sections.name: Prev Discussion
paragraphs: ...ISSUED AT ...503 AM AKST Wed Nov 25 2026
- Another front continues to move north across the panhandle bringing light rain and breezy winds with snow showers lingering for the northern panhandle.
- Multiple rounds of rain and wind are likely through the next few days with the possibility of some drier and cooler weather this weekend.

SHORT TERM.../Through Thursday night/ Yet another front is moving through the panhandle this morning. It is, as of 4 am, positioned over the central panhandle and is moving NW. A band of precipitation associated with it is currently bringing low elevation rain to areas from Angoon southward. Otherwise the main other effect is some increased winds as the feature moves through an area.

Into Thursday night, more fronts and troughs moving into the panhandle from the south remain the main forecast problem bringing periods of rain and some breezy conditions at times. Each is bringing its own bands of rain and some gusty at times winds. There are at least three of these features of note. The first is the current front moving through the panhandle this morning. That will continue to move NW and weaken as it goes.

Features number two comes into the southern panhandle this evening and looks to be the stronger of the three frontal features. Min gale force winds are possible out of Dixon entrance into the far SE gulf Thursday evening due to this feature and the southern panhandle could see some gusts to 35 mph at times. This front will work its way north through Thursday morning also weakening as it goes.

Feature number three is a weaker trough/remains of a low that approaches the southern panhandle Thursday into Thursday evening. This features is somewhat weak and will mostly bring another period of rain and some breezy winds at times.

LONG TERM...You heard it here first folks. Sunday looks like a pretty nice day across much of the Panhandle and coast. Expect winds to start dying off Friday as our parade of lows comes to an end, allowing high pressure to once again briefly dominate, increasing the odds for a little sun, primarily Sunday. The biggest question in the extended forecast is a shortwave trough moving in from the western Gulf Saturday, which has a decent signal of colder air associated with it. 850mb temperatures near -5C certainly make one ponder the rain/snow line for Icy Strait; however, the long transit over relatively warm ocean waters will help warm the surface airmass, along with onshore southerly flow scrubbing out colder air at the surface, likely limiting sea level impacts to rain. Something to track through the rest of this week if this system starts trending colder, which could mean a hit of snow for Icy Strait north. Either way on Sunday, mariners looking to make moves across the inner channels should enjoy lighter winds, keeping a close eye on major inlets like Taiya, Taku, and Stikine for breezy northerly to easterly winds. This may help prime some northern communities for additional snow later on next week.

For folks operating along the mighty Gulf coast, fresh seas will wind down Friday with long period southerly swell flourishing, becoming westerly by the end of the weekend. By and large significant wave heights should reach near or below 5 to 7 ft by Sunday, existing within a more comfortable long period swell spectrum. The exception may be waters west of Prince of Wales where we could see 7 to 9 ft fresh seas from higher northwesterly winds. Monday, the Aleutian Storm Track opens up opportunities for storm development into the Gulf into next week.

High confidence for lighter winds in the inner channels and the overall marine forecast thru Sunday. Keep an eye for fog in the forecast as we move closer to the weekend. The largest uncertainty in the long range is cold air advection on the backside of the shortwave trough Saturday which has implications on precipitation type for the north. As of Tuesday night, the published forecast reflects high confidence for rain Saturday with room to pivot if the system trends colder.

AVIATION.../Through Thursday morning/...A wave pushing northward across the panhandle continues to bring light precipitation to a majority of the panhandle Wednesday morning in the wake of the previous front Tuesday night. Light snow showers linger in the vicinity of Haines and Skagway, while the rest of the region remains warm enough to see rain at sea level. Conditions will generally improve across the northern panhandle with a break in precipitation Wednesday night though winds will pick up out of the north ahead of the next feature approaching from the south. As of this discussion, the southern half of the panhandle is continuing to see light rain behind the primary frontal passage, with otherwise VFR conditions as CIGs AoA 4000 ft. This is generally expected to hold true with the next system moving up from the south, bringing some gusty winds and potential for intermittent high end MVFR conditions by Wednesday afternoon and into Wednesday night. Overall the pattern will remain active over the next few days as a series of systems pass over or just offshore of the panhandle, with conditions primarily ranging from low end VFR to high end MVFR (between 2.5 and 3.5k ft). While some gusty winds will accompany the next system for the far southern panhandle and outer coast, there are no significant LLWS concerns for the period.

MARINE... Eastern Gulf of Alaska: A series of compact low pressure centers with remains of frontal bands moving SE to NW through the eastern gulf waters will be the main forecast concern into late week. Winds will mostly be 20 to 30 kt out of the E to SE through the next few days with the highest winds near the low centers as they move through an area. Strongest system will be Thursday evening in the far SE gulf featuring some min gale force winds coming out of Dixon Entrance due to a front in that area. Most of these winds will be in the near coastal waters within 100 nm from shore. Central gulf waters will see lighter winds. Seas generally expected to be between 10 and 15 ft through late week with a dominate SE swell of around 8 to 10 ft gradually subsiding into Friday.

Inner Channels: Northerly winds feature in the northern inner channels all the way down to Frederick Sound this morning. Wind speeds tend to vary between 15 and 25 kt with the higher winds being observed in advance of the northward moving frontal bands as northerly pressure gradients tighten. This will continue to be the case over the next few days as northerly winds continue and sometimes increase as frontal bands move north. Meanwhile the southern inner channels have been seeing mostly SE winds of 10 to 20 kt with occasional higher gusts to 30 kt mainly when the various fronts move through. This will also largely remain consistent through the next few days as well though there will be a period of winds up to 25 to 30 kt Wednesday evening as a stronger frontal feature moves through the area. Seas are mainly expected to remain around 3 to 5 ft for most areas with some higher waves to 7 ft in ocean entrances exposed to the S.

BOI.name: Boise
BOI.excerpt: The potential for a hard freeze in the Boise metro area appears to still not occur by early December. This would be the latest freeze on record, with the previous latest freeze occurring November 16th, 2016.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Rain and high-mountain snow in northern areas Thanksgiving Day. Cloudy, dry, and continued mild in the south, including the Snake Basin and southeast Oregon.
- Light rain Thursday night and Friday, mainly north, then heavier Friday evening and overnight. Snow above pass levels.
- Windy in southern areas Friday night during passage of a cold front.
- Dry but continued mild Saturday afternoon through Sunday.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: Cold front and scattered light rain showers dissipated in western ID this morning. The next Pacific frontal system was approaching the NW coast this afternoon, with light rain and high-mountain snow headed for the northern third of our CWA Thanksgiving Day. The rest of our CWA will be mostly cloudy but dry and continued mild. Rain and high-mountain snow will continue in ID north of the Snake Basin Thursday night due to orographic ascent of the moist westerly flow. There is a minimal (10-15%) chance of freezing rain in the colder valleys of western Baker County Friday morning, not impactful as we see it. On Friday the next Pacific upper trough will approach the NW coast. That trough looks more energetic than the one currently near the coast, and also wetter as it taps into sub- tropical Pacific moisture before making landfall. Friday night looks quite wet in our CWA as that system comes directly inland. Latest models have more QPF than before, .75 to 1.50 inch total pcpn Thursday morning through Friday night in the West-Central Idaho Mountains and Boise Mountains, .15 to .30 inch in southwest ID and eastern OR valleys, and .30 to .75 inch in higher southern mountains. Heaviest pcpn is expected Friday evening while snow level is still above 6000 feet. Therefore, we expect rain even at pass levels. Rain will change to snow overnight into Saturday morning down to 5200 feet behind a cold front, with several inches accumulation, still above most passes. Southern areas will become windy Friday night, especially in the Snake Basin SE of Boise and south to the ID/NV border, where west or southwest gusts to 45 mph are indicated ahead of and with passage of the cold front. Winds will decrease overnight.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: On the heels of the shortwave that moved through, upper-level ridging will bring high pressure Saturday and Sunday. Some lingering showers across SW Idaho will be ongoing to start Saturday, but will quickly taper off as dry conditions dominate both days. This dry period will be short-lived though, as another upper-level shortwave trough is forecast to move across the Pacific Northwest to start next week. Precipitation chances will begin to rise Sunday night with another push of valley rain and mountain snow. This system will bring slightly cooler temperatures and lower snow levels back down to 5000-6000 ft MSL. Ridging will attempt to build back in early Wednesday, but a closed low just off the California coast will move through the region, splitting the upper-level flow and bringing cooler air and precipitation back to the southern part of the area. Model uncertainty remains on the timing and positioning of the low, but most solutions and ensemble members agree that the bulk of the precipitation will be to our south over the Desert Southwest. Current forecast keeps a 20-40% chance of precipitation over the region through Wednesday, with temperatures lingering around 5-10 degrees above normal.

The potential for a hard freeze in the Boise metro area appears to still not occur by early December. This would be the latest freeze on record, with the previous latest freeze occurring November 16th, 2016.

BOU.name: Boulder / Denver
BOU.excerpt: Beyond that, dry weather is expected to redevelop by late Saturday night and hold through Sunday night. The next chance of snow would then start in the mountains by Monday or Monday night as a weakening disturbance pushes through the Central Rockies.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Gradual warming trend and dry weather through Friday.
- Gusty winds expected along the northern Front Range and northern border area Friday, spreading to all the plains Saturday.
- Snow and blowing snow in the mountains for Thanksgiving weekend return travel. Banded rain/snow showers possible for the plains and I-25 Corridor Saturday - Saturday night.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: Flat upper level ridging will keep dry conditions in place through Friday, along with a warming trend. For tonight, mid and high clouds will pass overhead but some late night clearing and a dry airmass should still support near normal low temperatures. Sunshine most of Thanksgiving Day and further upper level ridging, warming aloft, and weakening inversions will aid high temperatures warming several degrees above normal. We think most of the plains will be able to reach the 50s, coolest (near 50F) in the far northeast and warmest (approaching 60F) in Denver. Winds will remain light.

On Friday, the flow aloft will strengthen as an upper level low and associated shortwave move across southern Canada and the Northern Rockies, while an upper high holds over the east Central Pacific. That means increasing winds for our mountains and foothills, with gusts to 35-50 mph expected in wind prone areas. The northern plains near the Wyoming and Nebraska borders will also see winds increase with gusts to 30-35 mph. Fire weather conditions will be elevated due to the winds, but humidity levels are still forecast well above critical thresholds. Mid and upper level moisture will likely bring more clouds, and perhaps a couple light late day snow showers for the northern mountains. Snow showers will gradually increase in the mountains Friday night as orographics and moisture levels improve, with the heaviest snow and more significant post-Thanksgiving travel impacts expected by Saturday.

That heavier mountain snow (and blowing snow) will be driven by an upper level disturbance racing off the Pacific and across the Northern/Central Rockies on Saturday. We'll be getting into the left exit region of a 120 kt jet, with improving QG forcing, stronger orographics, and neutral lapse rates. Therefore, all the ingredients will be in place for at least a moderate snowfall event. The only ingredient that would be more uncertain at this point would be the moisture. Model and ensemble trends have generally been upward with QPF given the GFS and GEFS members were also coming more in line with the stronger/slightly farther south solution. Several inches of snow are now likely for the high country, with potential high end of over a foot in the northern Gore and Park Ranges. We'll likely need an Advisory for the mountains Friday night - Saturday night for the mountains, with possible Watch/Warning for the northern Gore/Park Ranges in upcoming forecast packages if the trends remain favorable. Saturday will not be the day for your post-Thanksgiving travel if heading through the Colorado mountains. Plan on Friday or Sunday (only lingering morning slick spots) for a safer journey.

For the plains and I-25 Urban Corridor, the depth and intensity of the trough offers up additional uncertainty in the forecast. Given the favorable ingredients mentioned above, it would not surprise us to see more widespread/numerous showers spread off the higher terrain. The highest odds of this happening would be behind the strong frontal surge on Saturday. If this can link up with the forcing of the upper level disturbance, then higher coverage and potential for banded snow would be possible. While most areas would likely see limited accumulations due to marginal temperatures, it should be noted that localized heavier bands of snow up to 2-4" would be possible (20-30% chance) in this scenario. We'll continue to monitor the forcing mechanisms and timing closely to see if they can link up.

Beyond that, dry weather is expected to redevelop by late Saturday night and hold through Sunday night. The next chance of snow would then start in the mountains by Monday or Monday night as a weakening disturbance pushes through the Central Rockies. The relatively active weather pattern (at least for the mountains) will likely remain in place with additional disturbances expected by mid week and another late next week. After a colder weekend, temperatures are expected to warm back a few degrees above normal next week.

CYS.name: Cheyenne
CYS.excerpt: Saturday will be fairly interesting as the day goes on. To start the morning it will be windy as the 700mb jet slowly starts moving south across the Colorado border.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - High winds are possible Thursday night through Saturday night. A High Wind Watch is currently in effect for the southeast Wyoming wind prone areas.
- Forecast uncertainty in regards to precipitation remains high for lower elevations over the weekend due to notable model variance, though mountain snow is likely.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: An overall quiet and pleasant day is expected across SE Wyoming and the Nebraska Panhandle, with little to no issues in terms of travel impacts ahead of Turkey Day tomorrow. A positively-tilted upper- level ridge is located over the western half of the United States, bringing us dry and seasonably mild conditions today across the region. For the time being, winds across the region are rather calm as a broad 1040+ mb anticyclone is located to our east and there is large-scale subsidence beneath the ridge. Based on current warming trends across the Nebraska Panhandle, increased high temperatures for today mainly along the I-80 corridor where we may manage to top 50 degrees given mostly sunny skies with just a few high clouds noted on visible satellite imagery. Expect another calm and cool night ahead, with partly to mostly cloudy skies as a weak shortwave trough and associated vorticity maximum skirts across the region with no precipitation expected.

Tomorrow will feature warmer and well-above average temperatures as the ridge builds over the Rocky Mountain West, resulting in a beautiful day to feast on turkey, mashed potatoes, pie, and everything else your heart desires. The gravy on top will be a noticeable increase in our wind speeds beginning during the late afternoon and early evening, especially for the wind-prone areas. This will be in part due to a broad mid-level open wave digging across the Canadian Prairies, acting to strengthen the meridional height gradient and therefore our wind speeds. WNW 700 mb flow is expected to ramp up to 60-65 knots overnight Thursday, with omega fields indicating a mountain wave pattern in place due to the cross-barrier flow. Vertical cross-sections across the Snowy and Sierra Madre Ranges demonstrate strong mountain-top stability especially within the 700- 600 mb layer, with unidirectional flow above. There isn't a consistent signal of drastically increasing or decreasing flow with height, so with the lack of any apparent mean-state critical layer (also due to no reversal in wind direction with height), so wave breaking in the lee of our mountain ranges won't be maximized, but 55-60 knot 700 mb Craig-Casper height gradients should compensate some for this. This is somewhat in-line with our in- house random forest guidance, which shows the wind-prone areas like Arlington and Bordeaux seeing anywhere from a 60 to 70 percent probability of experiencing high wind conditions into Friday morning, yet locations such as Cheyenne and Laramie are only sitting at around 10-15%. Current thinking is that it is reasonable for adjacent wind-prone areas to also see high wind conditions during this period, however this will highly depend on where any wave breaking takes place. As it stands, very much agree with the previous shift in issuing the High Wind Watch for the wind-prone areas into Friday morning. Overnight Thursday into Friday will also be quite mild thanks to all the turbulent mixing, with many locations (especially the wind-prone areas) remaining above freezing.

The windy conditions will prevail into Friday as WNW cross-barrier flow continues, with another day of dry and above-average temperatures expected. High wind conditions look to decrease for the wind-prone areas of the Laramie Range as weak forcing for ascent downstream of a weak shortwave embedded in NW flow aloft looks to erode the mountain-top stable layer. This is indicated on forecast soundings, with profiles also hinting at considerable mid and high- level cloud cover later on the day on Friday. The wind-prone areas along the I-80 corridor are a bit more uncertain at this time, as the bulk of the forcing for ascent will be situated to the north. With cross-barrier flow peaking around 60-65 knots, can expect the to see high wind conditions remain in place well into Saturday morning, with current random forest guidance showing 60% probabilities persisting in places like the I-80 Summit and Arlington. For this reason, the High Wind Watch for these locations extends well into Saturday before another pattern shift takes place to start out the long term period.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: Saturday will be fairly interesting as the day goes on. To start the morning it will be windy as the 700mb jet slowly starts moving south across the Colorado border. Our wind prone areas along I-80 and I-25 will continue to have high winds to borderline highs through the morning and early afternoon we will slowly see the winds start to drop in the afternoon hours as a cold front shifts the winds from their westerly direction to a more northerly direction after the cold front passes through. While the winds will still be rather breezy into the overnight hours, the possibility of high winds significantly decreases after 21z or 2pm Saturday. A mid-level open wave will also be pushing through Saturday morning on top of our High winds. While this system doesn't appear to be totally saturated there are some plumes of moisture that will be able to produce some snowfall from the synoptic forcing alone. Albeit the only places that are going to see the snowfall in our high wind westerly pattern will be the mountain peaks for Saturday morning and early afternoon. However, the cold front will be the deciding factor for everywhere expected to pass through the forecast area by the late afternoon. A strong vorticity gradient is associated with the cold front. The vorticity gradient is fairly strong enhancing the rain and snowfall rates. Areas east of I-25 will see a faster transition from rain to snow as the cold front will reach them first as its expected to kind of pinwheel are the Laramie range as well as having less downsloping winds compared to the Lower elevations west of the I-25 corridor. The biggest problem for the lower elevations (I-25 and east) will be overcoming the dry boundary layer set in place from the downsloping winds off the breaking mountain wave. Another factor for the lower elevations will be how fast the precipitation will change over from rain to snow. With 700mb temperatures dropping down to -10c behind the cold front, the transition should be fairly quick but getting the boundary layer to reach near saturation would be needed before any precip can reach the ground. This cold airmass behind the cold front unfortunately wont stay over us long as an upper level ridge will push into the area Sunday advecting in warmer air into the region. By Monday morning the lower elevations will be in the upper 40's to lower 50's and the higher elevations will be in the mid to upper 40's. These warmer temperatures are expected to continue through mid-week and likely melting any snow that accumulated that is not on the mountain top.

GJT.name: Grand Junction
GJT.excerpt: High pressure ridge moves back in for Sunday following the passage of this system with northwest flow setting up again on Monday as a weak clipper brushes to the north.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Mild and dry conditions expected through Thanksgiving.

- There is increasing confidence in active weather for the holiday weekend after Thanksgiving with the northern mountains being favored for snowfall. Exact details remain uncertain at this time. Stay tuned for updates to timing and impacts as they become available especially if traveling.
- An unsettled pattern looks to continue into next week with potential for more mountain snow but details remain uncertain.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: MILD AND DRY CONDITIONS THROUGH THANKSGIVING:

A shortwave ridge moving overhead will lead to dry and mild afternoon conditions. Upstream, high clouds continue to infiltrate across the area as a shortwave approaches from the west. All indications continue to point towards a split flow pattern with a closed low passing well south of Arizona and New Mexico, leaving us with just some passing mid and high cloud cover this evening into Thanksgiving morning with thin high clouds Thanksgiving Day and pleasant mild and dry conditions with temperatures around 5 to 10 degrees above normal. Some low level moisture with the colder nights may lead to patchy fog development overnight especially where clearing skies occur but low confidence due to passing cloud cover which would make this less likely.
POTENTIAL SYSTEM AFTER THANKSGIVING INTO THE WEEKEND:

Beyond Thanksgiving Day, moisture will begin moving into the Pacific Northwest and across the northern Rockies Friday into the weekend, setting up a northwest flow across the region as high pressure builds over the Desert Southwest just off the SoCal coast. The Park Range looks to receive the brunt of this moisture with a favored set up for northwest orographic snowfall Friday through Saturday, but more particularly Friday evening through Saturday night. While confidence is high that a weather system will impact the region, there are still some discrepancies on how far south the impacts will extend based on varying model solutions. We could see impacts down to Vail Pass especially into Saturday as a stronger piece of energy pushes through on the back side of the trough, but the Park Range looks to benefit the most from decent snow accumulations from this northwest orographic flow. Confidence is highest over the Park Range with lowering confidence to the south. Highlights may be needed but would like to see some better clarification on details before issuing any products depending on timing and amounts. Anyone traveling late this week and this weekend should prepare for potentially difficult conditions.

High pressure ridge moves back in for Sunday following the passage of this system with northwest flow setting up again on Monday as a weak clipper brushes to the north. There is a chance that northwest orographic flow could keep snow ongoing over the Park Range so this remains to be seen. Looking ahead, there are some indications of another system impacting the region mid to late next week but guidance diverges on specific scenarios. Regardless, it looks to remain unsettled.

PUB.name: Pueblo
PUB.excerpt: Overnight Monday into Tuesday, a band of 500mb vorticity, potentially overlapping with the right entrance region of a 300mb jet and a shortwave, could give another shot of snow to the mountains, particularly the Central Mountains.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Dry and mild through Friday, with temps in the 50s on Thanksgiving Day.
- Snow potential for Central Mountains Saturday.
- Low confidence in light snow for Palmer Divide Saturday night.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: Weak northwest flow aloft and upper level ridging will dominate the region, bringing dry, quiet weather today. High temperatures will reach the mid 40s in the mountains and the low 50s for the plains and valleys. Overnight, lows drop into the teens and low 20s across our region. For Thanksgiving, quiet weather will continue. Highs across the plains and valleys will reach the mid 50s, with some areas approaching 60.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: The next impactful weather day is Saturday, when the beginnings of a low pressure will sweep down from Wyoming, bringing northwesterly winds to our area. For the Central Mountains, the official forecast currently calls for 1-3 inches, but given the orographic effects, 3- 5 inches is now a stronger possibility, especially for Lake County. Other parts of the CWA below the mountaintops will start off as a light rain in the afternoon. As the low pressure moves further east, and the lower levels respond to a more northerly wind flow across the Palmer Divide, the Springs area may end with a light dusting of snow, or even some minor accumulations.

Overnight Monday into Tuesday, a band of 500mb vorticity, potentially overlapping with the right entrance region of a 300mb jet and a shortwave, could give another shot of snow to the mountains, particularly the Central Mountains. Wednesday night into Thursday could similarly give some snow to the Central and San Juan Mountains, likely being aided by a weak low pressure along the CO/KS border. The warmer than average pattern will make it harder to snow in the San Luis Valley, but for now, at least an inch is forecasted for the valley. Models do disagree on weather or not the Sangres/Wets get snow from this event, but all agree that anyone from Pueblo into the Eastern Plains will have to continue waiting for their first snowfall for the foreseeable future. Portions of the Eastern Plains could experience temperatures 10 degF above average later next week.

SLC.name: Salt Lake City
SLC.excerpt: Looking into the long term, it looks like we continue to avoid the development of a strong blocking ridge off the Pacific coast, and this will allow periodic storm systems to impact the area throughout next week.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Utah and southwest Wyoming will see dry conditions with temperatures near seasonal normals both today and Thanksgiving Day.
- More mild temperatures will move into the area for Friday, with high temperatures running 5-10F above seasonal normals as conditions stay dry.

- A weak weather system brushing by northern Utah Friday night through early Saturday will bring light valley rain and mountain snow mainly north of I-80. Temperatures will return to near seasonal normals for Saturday afternoon.
- More mild conditions will return for early next week with the potential for a more active pattern to set up for the latter half of the upcoming week.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: High pressure is centered near the Utah/Colorado border this morning with a weak trough moving onshore along the California coast. Earlier patchy fog has dissipated, with dry and seasonable conditions anticipated throughout the day. High clouds currently streaming across the area are expected to exit this evening into the overnight hours, and this clearly will allow for another opportunity for patchy fog in prone locations such as the Cache Valley and in the vicinity of the Great Salt Lake.

The California trough is expected to move southeast, keeping it well south of the area tonight into Thanksgiving Day. Thus, high pressure will continue to prevail, resulting in another dry and seasonable day tomorrow. With flow staying light, valley inversions will persist, resulting in some reduction in air quality. Flow aloft is on track to increase for Friday, allowing valley inversions to mix out and temperatures to trend upward, running 5-10F above seasonal normals.

Guidance is in good agreement that a weak Pacific northwest trough will move into northern portions of the area late Friday into Saturday, bringing generally light valley rain and mountain snow, primarily for areas north of I-80, as well as bringing temperatures back to near normal for this time of year. High pressure will then briefly build for Sunday before yet another weak storm system moves across northern Utah for Monday.

Looking into the long term, it looks like we continue to avoid the development of a strong blocking ridge off the Pacific coast, and this will allow periodic storm systems to impact the area throughout next week. Noticeable spread continues to exist in the guidance about the details of these systems, but current solutions are leaning toward more impactful storms for the area for the latter half of the upcoming week.

2660.travel_advice: Heightened avalanche conditions on specific terrain features. Evaluate snow and terrain carefully; identify features of concern.

product.author: Mike Walter
bottom_line: You can trigger a slab avalanche near and above treeline on the north half of the compass on slopes steeper than about 30 degrees. These avalanches can be large enough to bury or injury you. Give drifted slopes a wide berth; you might trigger them from above, next to, or below.
Seek out wind-sheltered areas and slopes below treeline for safer travel options.

2753.travel_advice: Heightened avalanche conditions on specific terrain features. Evaluate snow and terrain carefully; identify features of concern.

product.author: Ben Pritchett
bottom_line: You can still trigger a dangerous avalanche where you encounter older wind-drifted slabs below ridgelines, especially on northwest through north to east-facing slopes at upper elevations. You might trigger them from thin spots above, adjacent to, or below the drifted features. Choose wind-sheltered terrain to avoid the problem.

2754.travel_advice: Generally safe avalanche conditions. Watch for unstable snow on isolated terrain features.

product.author: Mike Walter
bottom_line: Most slopes are safe from avalanches due to thin and discontinuous snow cover. You can trigger a small avalanche in wind-drifted snow above treeline. Look for these drifts below ridges and around rocky outcrops on slopes facing west through north to east.

2755.travel_advice: Generally safe avalanche conditions. Watch for unstable snow on isolated terrain features.

product.author: Ian Fowler
bottom_line: Most slopes are safe to travel on as there is very little snow. In the alpine, steer around hard drifts of snow on steep terrain features and below ridgetops.

3046.travel_advice: Watch for signs of unstable snow such as recent avalanches, cracking in the snow, and audible collapsing. Avoid traveling on or under similar slopes.

1736.travel_advice: Watch for signs of unstable snow such as recent avalanches, cracking in the snow, and audible collapsing. Avoid traveling on or under similar slopes.

3014.travel_advice: Watch for signs of unstable snow such as recent avalanches, cracking in the snow, and audible collapsing. Avoid traveling on or under similar slopes.

product.author: Kevin Studley
bottom_line: Elevations above 7,000 feet have 1-2 feet of snow on the ground. You may encounter pockets of wind slabs above 7,500 feet on north- and east-facing terrain. If the snow feels stiff or slabby underfoot, then find a different aspect away from wind-drifted snow. The biggest hazard remains thin snow cover and hitting rocks, logs, and stumps. Even a small slide through thin coverage could end a season before it even starts.
We'll update the General Avalanche Information weekly until full-time forecasting operations begin.
hazard_discussion: Above 7,000 feet, a layered snowpack is beginning to build for the season. Good, albeit thin, skiing and riding conditions have been reported at upper elevations. Elevations below 7,000 feet remain thin and bony. Before November 13th, most slopes were bare. Winter trailhead access remains a challenge as there is not quite enough snow to launch sleds. Most forest roads become impassable by vehicle above 6,500 feet. As folks start poking around the mountains, remember that avalanches can occur with just a few feet of snow on the ground. There may be some lingering pockets of wind slabs above 7,500 feet on north and east-facing terrain features, particularly just below ridgelines.

Beginning Thanksgiving Day, a large storm system will impact the Pacific and Interior Northwest. Strong winds, mountain snow, and fluctuating rain/snow levels will be in the cards for several days. Pay attention to changing weather and snow conditions heading into the weekend. Stay up to date on mountain weather with our WEATHER tab, where you'll find webcams, weather stations, and weather forecasting tools.

Fresh wind slabs will come back onto the menu with more snow and wind later this week. Pay attention to gullies that can become crossloaded and may also act as a terrain trap. Look for clues of wind-affected snow, such as drifts, dunes, pillows, and freshly built cornices. Watch for signs of instability, such as shooting cracks. If you're observing these signs, find another aspect away from wind-drifted snow.
Turn On Your Snow and Avalanche Brain

• Beacons, shovels, probes, airbags. Run through all your gear and make sure it's functioning properly. Does your transceiver or airbag need any firmware updates? Look for cracks, defects, or corroded batteries. Make it fun with your friends and do a pre-season gear check with your winter travel companions.
• Check out the Education tab on our website to sign up for avalanche courses this winter (COURSES ).

• Help us paint a picture of what's going on in the mountains. If you're out in the mountains, submit an observation HERE. A simple photo and/or weather observation helps forecasters and the public alike.
